reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: A mucus extravasation or retention lesion arising from the sublingual gland, presenting as a soft cystic swelling in the floor of the mouth
The classic oral ranula appears as a bluish, dome-shaped, translucent swelling lateral to the midline that may fluctuate in size
It is termed a pseudocyst when it results from extravasated mucus without a true epithelial lining, the commonest mechanism
Large lesions can displace the tongue and interfere with speech, chewing and swallowing
Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by imaging to define extent and distinguish a simple oral ranula from a plunging variant
Definitive management usually involves excision of the sublingual gland along with the ranula, which addresses the source of mucus
Marsupialisation alone is associated with a higher recurrence rate than removal of the offending gland
Recurrence and the possibility of a plunging component should be considered when the lesion extends toward the neck
reference.pathophysiology: A ranula develops when saliva from the sublingual gland escapes into the surrounding floor-of-mouth tissues, most often because a duct or acinus is disrupted by trauma or obstruction. The extravasated mucus incites a surrounding reaction and collects as a pseudocyst lacking a true epithelial lining, though less commonly a true retention cyst forms behind a ductal obstruction. Continued salivary secretion causes the swelling to enlarge and fluctuate. If mucus tracks around or through the mylohyoid muscle into the neck, a cervical (plunging) ranula results.
additionalDifferentials: Dermoid or epidermoid cyst of the floor of mouth
Mucocoele of a minor salivary gland
Thyroglossal or branchial anomaly when near the midline or neck
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound of the floor of mouth and neck to characterise the cystic lesion
MRI or CT to delineate extent and detect a plunging component
Aspiration showing viscous, amylase-rich mucoid fluid where diagnosis is unclear
Histological examination of the excised specimen
Assessment of salivary gland duct anatomy when obstruction is suspected
redFlags: Rapid enlargement causing tongue displacement and difficulty with speech or swallowing
Airway compromise from a very large floor-of-mouth swelling
Features atypical for a simple ranula suggesting neoplasm
Extension into the neck indicating a plunging ranula
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent once the sublingual gland is removed, with low recurrence. Simple drainage or marsupialisation without gland removal is more likely to recur.
pitfalls: Treating with incision and drainage alone, which commonly leads to recurrence
Failing to recognise a plunging component presenting as a neck mass
Mistaking a solid salivary neoplasm for a benign cystic ranula
Injuring the lingual nerve or submandibular duct during sublingual gland excision
